02 · EXPLORE

Reading

Read the texts and answer the questions that follow.

READING 01

1. This passage is about DNA profiling.

Forensic science plays a major role in criminal investigations thanks to a technique for identifying DNA known as DNA profiling. This procedure identifies an individual's distinctive patterns of DNA. A DNA profile is the detailed analysis of the genetic material found in minuscule samples of human tissue or bodily fluid. In many countries, DNA profiles are kept on record in a national database. Initially, a sample can be obtained from biological evidence, such as bloodstains or strands of hair found at the scene of a crime. Then, should a sample be required from a suspect, police usually ask for saliva. Following analysis, if a DNA sample matches an existing profile in the database, it can confirm the identity of the perpetrator, since the likelihood of one profile matching two unrelated individuals is one in a billion. However, if no exact match emerges, but a profile in the database is similar to one found at a crime scene, it could belong to a close relative of the offender. Criminals have been tracked down via blood relations whose profiles closely resemble their own.

DNA profiling was developed in the 1980s by geneticist Alec Jeffreys. He had intended it as a means of screening people for hereditary diseases and genetic defects. Realizing the crime-solving potential of DNA profiling, the police requested his help in a murder case. Not only did DNA help identify the perpetrator, it also eliminated a different man as the prime suspect, who might otherwise have been wrongly convicted. Soon, DNA profiling was being used by police everywhere, and now many countries maintain national DNA databases. The largest, funded by the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), contains profiles of over one million habitual offenders convicted of or facing charges of certain types of federal crimes. To date, it has assisted in thousands of investigations.

The concept of a DNA database is not without its critics, however. Some governments retain DNA samples taken from people who were arrested but subsequently acquitted or released without charge. Civil rights advocates argue that this infringes on civil liberties and that only the profiles of convicted criminals should be kept on record.

READING 02

2. This passage is about a conservation project.

The biblical story of Noah's Ark tells of a large sailing vessel built to save animals and birds from a massive flood. Today too, thousands of mammal and bird species face imminent extinction due to human proliferation, urban expansion, and the rampant destruction of ecosystems. In response to this crisis, a project called the Frozen Ark is underway, with the aim of deep-freezing the DNA of all endangered animals. DNA is a template containing the complete specifications of an organism and is thus a treasure trove of knowledge about the organism and the species as a whole.

Until the Frozen Ark's creation, a major problem facing zoologists was that when a species became extinct, the knowledge of its genetic code was lost. However, specimens of skin tissue, embryos, sperm, and eggs are now being collected from animals on the most-endangered list, meaning important information about each animal's biology, behavior, ecology, and evolution can now be preserved. At low temperatures, DNA can remain intact indefinitely; once frozen, molecules and cells can be safeguarded for centuries to come. Scientists can therefore continue studying a species, even after it is extinct.

Furthermore, as a species declines, the fewer specimens there are. Consequently, the gene pool becomes more limited, which has an adverse effect on its genetic diversity. Freezing cells may enable biologists to reverse the dangerous loss of genetic variation that causes infertility and early death in such species. In addition, the cells of certain animals are proving effective in the treatment of some diseases. Should these animals die out, the benefits provided by their cells can be maintained. And when extinction does occur, if an animal's reproductive cells have been stored, it could theoretically be recreated by implanting the cells in a surrogate mother of a different species. One day, albeit not in the foreseeable future, it may even be possible to reconstruct an extinct animal from its DNA alone.

However, time is of the essence. Of the thousands of animal species facing extinction within the next 50 years, samples from only a small portion have been collected to date. The Frozen Ark project hopes to train researchers around the world so they will know how to collect and freeze biological materials before it's too late.

B — WILDLIFE FORENSICS

Read the text and replace the words in bold with the words below that have a similar meaning.

emerge • obtain • assist • track down • confirmed • released • convicted • strand • procedure • perpetrator • albeit • crime scene

Forensic science is now a standard part of police work. It is also used to investigate crimes involving animals, (1) though more rarely. When a grizzly bear was shot and killed in Alberta, Canada some years ago, park rangers immediately launched an investigation to (2) search for and find the individual responsible. A witness soon came forward with information, but the investigators knew that without conclusive evidence, the (3) person who committed the crime might never be (4) found guilty in court.

Fortunately, a (5) single piece of animal hair was discovered in a truck belonging to the prime suspect. A DNA sample was taken and analyzed. When this (6) set of actions was complete, the results (7) firmly established that this was, indeed, a grizzly bear hair. What's more, it was an exact match for the DNA that was extracted from a bone found at the (8) location of the crime. This was sufficient evidence to prove that the suspect had been involved in the illegal killing of the bear.

Wildlife forensics, as this field is known, can also (9) prove helpful in investigations into bear attacks on humans. When such incidents take place in a national park, rangers (10) get a DNA sample from any genetic material left behind by the animal, such as saliva or hair. Rangers then tranquilize any bears they find in the area of the attack and hold them in cages while their DNA is tested. If the result is negative, the bear will be (11) set free. However, if an exact DNA match should (12) result, the aggressive animal is usually put down.
